newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal's privatisations to exceed goal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal's privatisations to exceed goal.

text.p: Portugal's privatisation programme in 1997 is dominated by the sale of a stake in energy company EDP and is expected to surpass the state's revenue target of 410 billion escudos ($2.6 billion), analysts said on Thursday.

The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has announced an ambitious privatisation programme for 1997 that includes the selloff of a 25 to 30 percent stake in EDP-Electricidade de Portugal in the first half of the year.
Other selloffs will include stakes in oil company Petrogal, telecommunications group Portugal Telecom, pulp company Portucel Industrial and chemical group Quimigal-Quimica de Portugal SA.
Airport company ANA and motorway firm Brisa are also for sale in 1997, as well as shipbuilder Estaleiros Navais de Viana do Castelo SA and dredging company Dragapor-Dragagens de Portugal SA.
"The government should reach its revenue target," said Elizabeth Rothfield, partner with Lisbon broker Midas. "Most of that figure will be EDP."
Local media has reported that EDP had been valued at between 1,000 and 1,700 billion escudos.
A 25 percent stake worth between 250 and 425 billion escudos and a 30 percent stake worth between 300 and 510 billion escudos would be in the government's 410 billion escudo target range.
The Portuguese state earned at least 460 billion escudos from its privatisation programme in 1996, well above its revenue goal of 380 billion escudos.
Analysts said EDP's position as a monopoly producer of energy in Portugal and the success of utilities privatisations abroad would guarantee the selloff of the EDP stake.
"The success of the government's privatisation programme this year will hinge on EDP," said Mark Howard of Lloyds Bank Fund Managers in Cascais near Lisbon.

Saudi oil company Saudi Aramco had written to Petrogal-Petroleos de Portugal to say it planned to enter direct talks with the Portuguese company to buy a stake of about 35 percent, a source involved in the process said.

The third stage privatisation of Portugal Telecom in the second half of 1997 will include the sale of a 26 percent stake and the state will keep a 25 percent "golden share", Planning Minister Joao Cravinho said this week.
He said a partner could take a small percentage of PT.
PT's president Murteira Nabo said in a press interview last weekend that the firm expected to form a strategic alliance with a European partner or partners in March.
The government sold off 49 percent of PT in two stages in 1995 and 1996. PT shares have since surged on Lisbon and New York stock markets.
The timing of the privatisation of Portucel Industrial would depend on conditions in the highly cyclical pulp market and plans to restructure the sector, analysts said.
Since the sale of a 40 percent stake in the group in June 1995, the share has been a disappointing investment and remains below its privatisation price of 1,040 escudos per share.
Cravinho said this week that state airport company ANA-Aeroportos e Navegacao Aera was undergoing a reorganisation before a privatisation expected in late 1997.

He said two new companies would be created from the present ANA -- one to handle air traffic control, which would remain a public company, and the other to run airport facilities, which would be privatised.
Howard said he believed the government would have no difficulty privatising ANA as tourism in Portugal was set to grow, boosted by the 1998 Expo World Fair in Lisbon.
Under-Secretary for Finance Fernando Teixeira dos Santos said in a press interview last November that it may be possible to privatise motorway compay Brisa in the first half of 1997.
Brisa already operates valuable concessions to build several key roads in Portugal.
